337.title: Not things, but judgments
337.hook: people are upset not by things but by their judgments about things (Enchiridion 5)
337.tomorrow: The horse is handsome, not you
337.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often separate what happened from the judgment they've added to it, sometimes writing the two side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus, going to the baths. Your line was and keep my purpose. Did you add those words before walking through a door? Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Two people are stuck in the same traffic jam, same lane, same minute. One is pounding the wheel, already rehearsing the apology to the boss. The other has turned up the radio and is singing badly. Same cars. Same delay. Same red brake lights stretching to the bridge. So what, exactly, is upsetting the first driver? If it were the traffic, it would be upsetting both of them. Section five of the handbook gives Epictetus' answer, and it fits in a single breath. Today: not things, but judgments.
screen: `TWO DRIVERS, ONE JAM.` → `ONE FURIOUS, ONE SINGING.` → `WHAT'S DOING THE UPSETTING?`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." The Greek word for those opinions is dogmata, the plural of today's word. Second, the word. We hear dogma and think of rigid doctrine, something you're not allowed to question. In Epictetus' Greek it's humbler. It comes from a verb meaning to seem. A dogma is what seems so to you: your view, your verdict, the judgment you've already passed before you notice you passed it. The traffic is a thing. I'm going to be fired, this always happens to me: those are dogmata. Third, his example. Death, he says, isn't terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates, who faced his own calmly. The terrible part is the judgment that death is terrible. You can disagree with him about death and still try the move on a parking ticket. Then he adds a ladder. An untrained person blames others when things go badly. Someone starting out blames themself. Someone trained blames neither. Fourth, the long echo. The novelist Laurence Sterne put this sentence, in Greek, at the front of Tristram Shandy. And in the twentieth century the psychologist Albert Ellis named Epictetus as an influence on his therapy, which taught people to catch the belief that sits between an event and the feeling. Here is the honest limit. Epictetus isn't saying pain is imaginary or that nothing out there is wrong. He's saying the part that churns inside is built partly from our own verdicts. And a verdict can be looked at again.
screen: `NOT THE THINGS, BUT THE OPINIONS.` · `DOGMA: WHAT SEEMS SO TO ME.` · `SOCRATES, AND THE LADDER OF BLAME.` · `FROM STERNE TO THE THERAPY ROOM.` · then, large: `IT'S MY VIEW.`

segments.voice: Bring back one thing that upset you this week. Something small is fine: a text, a delay, a look. First, describe only what happened, the way a camera would see it. He replied with one word. The train came twelve minutes late. Then find the judgment underneath. He's annoyed with me. My whole day is ruined. Say it plainly, and then add: it's my view. Don't argue with it yet. Just see that it's a view, sitting there. The bell holds the time.
Dogma. In Epictetus' Greek, not rigid doctrine but a judgment, what seems so to you. It's our dogmata, he says, that disturb us. Today's word.
Your line: it's my view. The next time something stings today, split it in two: what happened, and what I'm saying about it. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

screen: `DAY 337 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HORSE IS HANDSOME, NOT YOU.`

338.title: The horse is handsome, not you
338.hook: don't boast about your fine horse, as if its beauty were yours (Enchiridion 6)
338.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism notice when they take credit for something they merely own or stand near, and remind themselves that their own part is how they respond.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dogma, the judgment underneath the upset. Your line was it's my view. When something stung, did you split it in two? Day three hundred thirty-eight.

A man pulls into a parking lot in a very shiny car and takes a little longer than necessary to get out of it. A parent mentions, for the third time at dinner, which college the kid got into. A fan says we won last night, about a team he has never played for. Each one is standing next to something fine and letting a little of its shine land on them. Epictetus noticed it in the ancient equivalent: the man with the beautiful horse. Today: the horse is handsome, not you.
screen: `THE SHINY CAR.` → `WE WON LAST NIGHT.` → `THE MAN WITH THE BEAUTIFUL HORSE.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Section six of the handbook says: don't be lifted up by an excellence that isn't yours. Second, the joke inside it. If the horse itself were proud, Epictetus says, and announced, I am beautiful, that would be bearable. The horse is, after all, beautiful. But when you say, I have a beautiful horse, and puff up, you're proud of the horse's good, not yours. The mane, the speed, the gleam: those belong to the animal. You're just the one holding the rope. Third, his question. So what is yours? His answer is a short phrase: the use of impressions. Every moment, things appear to you, a horse, an insult, a compliment, a fear. What you do with those appearances, how you judge them and respond, that's yours. When you handle them well, in line with nature, he says, then go ahead and be glad, because then you're glad about a good that's really your own. Fourth, why it matters on a Tuesday. Borrowed pride is fragile. The car gets scratched. The team loses. The kid has a hard year and suddenly your sense of yourself wobbles along with theirs. Epictetus isn't saying don't enjoy the horse, or don't love the kid, or don't cheer. He's saying keep the accounts straight. The horse is handsome. Your part is what you did today with what showed up. That can't be scratched in a parking lot.
screen: `AN EXCELLENCE NOT YOUR OWN.` · `IF THE HORSE SAID I AM BEAUTIFUL.` · `YOURS: THE USE OF IMPRESSIONS.` · `BORROWED PRIDE IS FRAGILE.` · then, large: `THE HORSE IS HANDSOME.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you feel a little proud of that isn't strictly yours. A possession, a title, where you went to school, a famous relative, a city, a team. Picture it clearly. Then give the credit back with Epictetus' sentence: the horse is handsome. Say the real name in place of horse. Notice whether anything in you shrinks or relaxes. Then ask: what did I actually do this week that was mine? Let one small answer come. The bell holds the time.
The horse is handsome. Epictetus' reminder that the shine of what we own or stand near belongs to it, not to us; ours is how we meet things. Today's word.
Your line: the horse is handsome. Catch one borrowed pride today, in yourself, gently. Say the line, and let the horse keep its own shine. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

339.title: When the captain calls
339.hook: ashore on a voyage you may gather shells, but when the captain calls, run to the ship (Enchiridion 7)
339.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners enjoy small pleasures while keeping in mind that they may be called away from them, and practice setting them down easily.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the horse is handsome, not you. That was also your line. Did you catch one borrowed pride and give the shine back? Day three hundred thirty-nine.

A ship drops anchor off a rocky island. Fresh water is low, so the crew rows a few passengers ashore with jars to fill at a spring. The beach is lovely. There are shells in the shallows, and wild onions growing in the dunes. Someone kneels to dig one up. Someone else wanders down the shore after a bigger shell. Out on the water, the captain is watching the wind turn. Any minute now, a shout will come across the bay. Epictetus tells this little story in section seven of the handbook. Today: when the captain calls.
screen: `AN ISLAND, A SPRING, A BEACH.` → `SHELLS AND WILD ONIONS.` → `THE WIND TURNS.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. On a voyage, Epictetus says, when the ship is at anchor and you go ashore for water, you may pick up a shellfish or a little bulb along the way. Nothing wrong with that. But keep your mind on the ship, and keep turning around to listen for the captain. If he calls, drop everything and run, or you'll be hauled on board tied up like the sheep. Second, the turn. So it is in life, he says. If instead of a bulb and a shell you're given a spouse and a child, nothing stops you having them. But if the captain calls, run to the ship and leave them behind, without looking back. And if you're old, don't wander far from the ship at all, or you may not make it when you're called. Third, what the call is. The handbook doesn't spell it out. Some readers hear the captain as God or the order of nature, and the call as death. Others hear any moment that asks you to let go. It's a stark picture, and some readers find the family line hard to hear. Others notice what it allows: you may gather. Love, collecting, beauty on the beach. The Stoic only asks that you keep one ear on the water. Fourth, the word. The Greek for the captain is kybernetes, the one who steers. Dictionaries trace English govern back to it, through Latin gubernare. Someone else is steering the ship. Your job ashore is simpler. Enjoy the beach. Fill your jar. Listen.
screen: `ASHORE: SHELLS AND BULBS ARE FINE.` · `IN LIFE: A SPOUSE, A CHILD.` · `WHAT IS THE CALL?` · `KYBERNETES: THE ONE WHO STEERS.` · then, large: `LISTEN FOR THE CALL.`

segments.voice: Think of one pleasure you'll pick up today. A coffee, a show, a scroll, a long lunch, an afternoon with someone you like. Hold it in your mind, and enjoy it there. Then picture the shout across the water: the moment it's time to stop. Picture yourself setting it down easily, the way you'd drop a shell back in the sand, and walking on. Breathe, and keep one ear turned toward the ship. The bell holds the time.
Kybernetes, the Greek for the ship's captain: gather shells and bulbs ashore if you like, but keep listening, and when the call comes, go. Today's word.
Your line: listen for the call. Enjoy one pleasure fully today, and when it's time to stop, put it down the first time you're called. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

screen: `DAY 339 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WISH IT AS IT COMES.`

340.title: Wish it as it comes
340.hook: don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish them as they happen (Enchiridion 8)
340.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often try to accept what has already happened as it is, while still putting full effort into what is up to them next.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kybernetes, when the captain calls. Your line was listen for the call. Did you put one pleasure down the first time you were called? Day three hundred forty.

You planned a picnic. It rains. You can spend the afternoon at the window, arguing with the sky, replaying the forecast that said ten percent. Or you can spread the blanket on the living room floor and eat the sandwiches there, listening to the rain on the roof. Same rain, either way. The difference is which direction your wishing points. Toward the day you wanted, or toward the day that came. Section eight of the handbook flips the usual arrow of wishing around. Today: wish it as it comes.
screen: `THE PICNIC, THE RAIN.` → `ARGUING WITH THE SKY.` → `WHICH WAY DOES THE WISH POINT?`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's translation: "Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life." Second, the flip. The usual order is to wish first and then wait to see if the world agrees. Epictetus says let the world go first. Then wish for what came. It sounds like a trick, and in a way it is: a way of making sure your wishes and the world never fight. The prize he names is a smooth flow: the Greek verb pictures a stream running without snags. Third, an older Stoic image. A later Christian writer, Hippolytus, reports that the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus compared us to a dog tied to a cart. If the dog wants to follow, it walks along, both pulled and willing. If it doesn't, it's dragged anyway. Either way the cart goes. The only choice is whether to trot or be dragged. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. This isn't Epictetus telling anyone to welcome cruelty or stop working for change. The handbook already sorted things into two piles. Your choices, your effort, your voice: those are yours, and you use them fully. What it asks is that once something has actually happened, the rain, the canceled flight, the result, you stop demanding it be otherwise. Centuries later the philosopher Nietzsche put a cousin of this idea into two Latin words: amor fati, love of fate. Epictetus' version is plainer. Not love, necessarily. Just: as it comes.
screen: `SEEK NOT THAT THINGS HAPPEN AS YOU WISH.` · `LET THE WORLD GO FIRST.` · `THE DOG AND THE CART.` · `WHAT IT DOESN'T MEAN.` · then, large: `AS IT COMES.`

segments.voice: Sit and listen for a moment to whatever is happening around you right now. A car, a fan, a voice in the next room, maybe silence. Don't wish any of it different. Let each sound arrive, and quietly wish it to be exactly as it is. Then bring to mind one small surprise from today that you didn't plan. A delay, a message, a change of weather. Turn toward it the same way, and say inside: as it comes. The bell holds the time.
Amor fati, love of fate: don't ask things to happen as you wish; wish them as they happen, and life flows. Today's word.
Your line: as it comes. When today surprises you, even a little, say the line before you say anything else, and see what's possible from there. Day three hundred forty.

341.title: The leg, not the will
341.hook: illness hinders the body, not the will; lameness hinders the leg, not you (Enchiridion 9)
341.tomorrow: What do I have for this?
341.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism, especially while ill or injured, name what a limit actually hinders and remind themselves of what remains theirs to choose.

segments.voice: Yesterday: amor fati, wish it as it comes. Your line was as it comes. When the day surprised you, did you say it first? Day three hundred forty-one.

This teacher knew bodily limits from the inside. The ancient sources agree that Epictetus walked with a limp, and they disagree about why. A critic named Celsus, quoted by the Christian writer Origen, tells a story that his master twisted his leg, and Epictetus said calmly, you'll break it, and when it broke, said, didn't I tell you? The philosopher Simplicius says only that he was lame from his youth. Nobody knows which is true. What we do know is that the man with the limp is the teacher behind section nine. Today: the leg, not the will.
screen: `A TEACHER WITH A LIMP.` → `TWO STORIES, NO CERTAINTY.` → `THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Illness, section nine says, is a hindrance to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is a hindrance to the leg, but not to the will. Second, the word. The will here is prohairesis, a word Epictetus returns to again and again. It means the power to choose: to assent or refuse, to judge, to set an aim. For him it's the real self, the part nothing outside can force. Third, the habit he asks for. Say this, he writes, about everything that happens to you. You'll find it's a hindrance to something else, but not to yourself. The flight is delayed: a hindrance to the schedule. The voice is gone: a hindrance to the speech. A diagnosis: a hindrance to the body. Each time, a quiet second clause: not to the will. Fourth, the honest limit. Modern readers sometimes push back here, and fairly. Pain, illness, exhaustion and depression can reach the mind, cloud judgment, make choosing itself hard. Epictetus isn't pretending a broken leg doesn't hurt. His claim is narrower and stubborn: even inside real limits, something remains to be decided. How to bear it, what to make of it, who to be while it lasts. Some people living with long illness find that line steadying; others find it too tidy. Both reactions are honest. And it helps to remember whose teaching it is: a man who, for one reason or another, spent his life walking on a bad leg.
screen: `A HINDRANCE TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `SAY IT ABOUT EVERYTHING.` · `THE HONEST LIMIT.` · then, large: `NOT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: Notice your body right now, top to bottom. Find one limit in it: a stiff back, tired eyes, an old injury, a cold. Name it plainly: this is a hindrance to my back. Then ask what it can't touch. Can it stop you choosing how to speak today? Being patient? Paying attention to this breath? Name one thing the limit doesn't reach, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
The leg. In section nine, the thing a limit actually hinders, the leg, the body, the plan, while the will, the power to choose, stays free. Today's word.
Your line: not the will. When something blocks you today, name what it really hinders, then add the second clause: not the will. Day three hundred forty-one.

342.title: What do I have for this?
342.hook: for each event, ask which power you have to meet it: patience for insult, endurance for hard work (Enchiridion 10)
342.carry: feel its weight in your hand
342.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners meet a difficulty by asking which strength it calls for, such as patience, endurance or courage, before reacting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the leg. Your line was not the will. When something blocked you, did you name what it really hindered? Day three hundred forty-two.

A plumber shows up at a flooded basement. She doesn't stand in the doorway saying, why me, why water, why today. She opens her bag. Wrench, tape, a pump. The question in her head is practical: what do I have for this? Most of us meet trouble the other way round. We describe it, complain about it, replay it. Epictetus suggests carrying a bag like the plumber's, only the tools are inside you. Section ten of the handbook is the moment you open it. Today: what do I have for this?
screen: `A FLOODED BASEMENT.` → `THE PLUMBER OPENS HER BAG.` → `WHAT DO I HAVE FOR THIS?`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. With everything that happens to you, Epictetus says, turn toward yourself and ask what power you have for dealing with it. The word for power is dynamis, the root English borrowed for dynamic and dynamite. Second, his three examples. If you see someone very beautiful and feel the pull, you'll find you have self-control for that. If hard work lands on you, you'll find endurance. If someone insults you, you'll find patience. Three troubles, three tools, each already in the bag. Third, the claim underneath. Notice what he's assuming: that for every kind of event, there's some human strength that fits it. Not that you'll enjoy it. That you're equipped for it, at least a little, and the equipment gets stronger with use. Elsewhere in the Discourses he says something similar in a sharper way: difficulties are what show who people are. Fourth, the habit. If you get used to asking the question, he says, the impressions won't carry you off. That's the key word: carried off. Without the question, a hard day picks you up and runs. With it, there's a pause, a hand reaching into the bag, and a choice of tool. You might find patience is thin today, or endurance is low. Fine. Asking still turns you from someone things happen to into someone deciding how to meet them. And the list is longer than three. Courage for a hard phone call. Gentleness for a child melting down. Humor for a ruined dinner. Honesty for a mistake at work.
screen: `TURN TO YOURSELF AND ASK.` · `BEAUTY, LABOR, INSULT.` · `A STRENGTH FOR EVERY TROUBLE.` · `NOT CARRIED OFF.` · then, large: `WHAT DO I HAVE FOR THIS?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one trouble you're carrying this week. A deadline, a difficult person, a worry, an ache. See it clearly for a moment. Then ask Epictetus' question slowly: what do I have for this? Wait. Let a word come: patience, courage, humor, honesty, rest. Picture taking that one tool out of the bag and holding it. You don't need to use it yet. Just feel its weight in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Dynamis, the power or strength Epictetus asks us to find for every event: self-control, endurance, patience, or another. Today's word.
Your line: feel its weight in your hand. When the next hard thing arrives today, ask what tool fits it, and reach for one. Day three hundred forty-two.

343.title: I gave it back
343.hook: never say "I lost it," say "I returned it" (Enchiridion 11)
343.carry: care for it like an inn
343.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism speak of a loss as something returned rather than lost, and try to care for what they have as a guest cares for an inn.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dynamis, what do I have for this? Your line was feel its weight in your hand. When something hard arrived, did you reach into the bag for one tool? Day three hundred forty-three, the end of a week.

Hotel checkout. A good night's sleep, a view, maybe the little soaps tucked in a bag. The key card goes back across the desk, and the room stays behind. Nobody calls that a loss. The room was never ours. We were guests. Now notice how differently we talk about almost everything else. I lost my job. I lost my wallet. I lost my grandmother. Section eleven of the handbook takes aim at one small verb, and suggests trading it for another. Today: I gave it back.
screen: `HANDING BACK THE KEY CARD.` → `I LOST IT.` → `ONE SMALL VERB.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In George Long's translation: "Never say about anything, I have lost it; but say I have restored it." Restored in the old sense: given back, returned. Second, how far he takes it. Epictetus doesn't stop at wallets. Your child has died? It was given back. Your land was taken? That too was given back. It's a hard passage, and he doesn't soften it. Some readers find comfort there, a way of holding grief inside gratitude. Others feel it asks too much too soon. Both are honest responses, and nobody has to decide today. Third, the objection. Someone in the handbook protests: but the person who took my land is a crook. Epictetus answers: what does it matter to you which hand the giver used to ask for it back? It's a hard reply, and an interesting one. It moves attention from the thief to the gift. Fourth, the inn. While it's given to you, he says, take care of it as something not your own, the way travelers treat an inn. Not carelessly. Travelers can love an inn. But they don't carve their name into the door. Neighbors know this turn of phrase. In the book of Job, after terrible news, Job says: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." A different home, a different understanding of who gives, a similar turn of thought. And a look back at this week: dogma, the horse, the captain, as it comes, the leg, the bag of tools, and today, the key card handed back.
screen: `NEVER SAY I HAVE LOST IT.` · `EVEN THE HARDEST LOSSES.` · `WHICH HAND ASKED FOR IT BACK?` · `CARE FOR IT LIKE AN INN.` · then, large: `I GAVE IT BACK.`

segments.voice: Think of one small loss from this year. Not the biggest. Something you can hold without breaking: a job, a friendship that faded, a phone, a place you moved away from. Say it the usual way first, inside: I lost it. Notice how that sits. Then try Epictetus' verb: I gave it back. Say it slowly. If it feels false, let it be false; just notice. If it brings a little thanks for having had it, stay with that. The bell holds the time.
Job, who said the Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away: Epictetus' trade of verbs, not I lost it, but I gave it back. Today's word.
Your line: care for it like an inn. The next time you're about to say I lost it today, even about keys, try the other verb instead. Another week on the porch done. Day three hundred forty-three.

myth: Epictetus applies this only to small things like wallets
he applies it to land, and even to a child who has died.
he says to care for what you have the way travelers treat an inn
with care, as something not your own.
Job says 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away'
in the King James words, Job 1:21.

fork.setup: your land has been taken by a dishonest neighbor. 'but he's a crook!' you say. how does Epictetus answer?
options: then take it back by force.
what is it to you which hand the giver used to ask for it back?
fork.reveal: he turns attention from the thief to the gift: it was given to you, and it has been asked back.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 11: I gave back, I returned.

trapdoor: what you thought: look on the bright side.
what it means: say I returned it, not I lost it, and care for what you have like a guest at an inn.
what a scholar hears: apedoka, I gave back, set against apolesa, I lost; Marcus Aurelius also calls life a stranger's sojourn (Meditations 2.17).

sources.ref: Enchiridion 11 (child, land, the taker, the inn)
